fixes.explanation: Guilt. Abimelech says, “One of the people could easily have slept with your wife, and you would have brought guilt upon us.” (Gen 26:10) I think he's rattled by what could have happened. Isaac had said she was his sister, and the king did NOT take that lightly.

Yes. “…the Philistines took dirt and stopped up all the wells that his father’s servants had dug in the days of his father Abraham.” (Gen 26:15) Those wells went back to Abraham, Isaac's father. Dirt was the tool, and it was all of the wells. That's a LOT of shoveling, and I've done my share of digging out of a drawer, so I respect the effort.

Yes, the herdsmen of Gerar. Isaac's servants had found a well of fresh water in the valley (Gen 26:19). Then Gerar's herdsmen quarrel with Isaac's herdsmen and say, “The water is ours!” (Gen 26:20) Isaac named the well Esek, because they contended with him. Somebody found water and somebody else filed a claim. I've seen that kind of thing over a parking spot.
Nope, Isaac isn't talking about his flocks and herds. He says, “You hated me and sent me away.” (Gen 26:27) That's about how they treated him, not what they took. Short and it lands.

Mocking isn't what Isaac says. He first asks, “Why have you come to me?” and then tells them, “You hated me and sent me away.” (Gen 26:27) Nothing about his God or his altar comes up in those words. Hated and sent away is the whole charge, and I think it carries plenty of sting by itself.

problems.problem: It has 6 sentences. Explanations are 3 to 5 sentences.
Isaac's awareness of that possible consequence is not given in the text.
Saying the Philistines stopped up the wells 'just to make a point' assigns them a reason the text does not give.
Isaac is pictured with his arms crossed, a posture the text does not give.
The text gives Isaac more words to them here: he also asks why they have come to him.
